```{r init_setup, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
# Include setup
library(tidyverse)
library(ggfortify)
library(knitr)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center"
)

hook_output <- knit_hooks$get("output")
knit_hooks$set(output = function(x, options) {
  lines <- options$output.lines
  if (is.null(lines)) {
    return(hook_output(x, options))  # pass to default hook
  }
  x <- unlist(strsplit(x, "\n"))
  more <- "..."
  if (length(lines) == 1) {        # first n lines
    if (length(x) > lines) {
      # truncate the output, but add ....
      x <- c(head(x, lines), more)
    }
  } else {
    x <- c(more, x[lines], more)
  }
  # paste these lines together
  x <- paste(c(x, ""), collapse = "\n")
  hook_output(x, options)
})
```

```{r, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
banco = read.csv("class_07_docs/banco.csv")
options(scipen = 999)

# Helpers used for inline values in the slides
sgn = function(x, d = 2) sprintf("%+.*f", d, x)          # signed number, e.g. +0.41 / -0.59
pct = function(b, d = 2) round((exp(b) - 1) * 100, d)    # percent change in the odds
dir = function(b) ifelse(b > 0, "increase", "decrease")  # direction of a change
```

## Quick review of our Class

This is what we covered in previous classes:

- [Simple and Multiple Regression]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- [Categorical Variables and Interactions]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- [Residual Analysis]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- [Time Series]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- [Model Selection]{style="color:darkorange;"}

Today we will introduce a [*new model*]{style="color:darkorchid;"}.

## The Banco data set {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The `banco` data set contains information about `r nrow(banco)` customers of a bank that extends **lines of credit**.
- We have data on customer [*age*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, [*number of dependents*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, [*sex*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, [*years in current job*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, [*years in current home*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, [*other lines of credit*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, and whether the account is in good standing.
- Let’s see if we can predict the `Status` of the account based on the customer's `Age`. (In this data set, every account is classified as [Good]{style="color:darkorange;"} or [Bad]{style="color:darkorange;"}.)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
banco %>% 
  select(Status, Age, Other_Credit) %>% 
  head(8) %>% 
  kable()
```
:::
:::::

## Let's build the model

- What’s wrong with this regression?

$$
\widehat{\text{Status}} = \widehat{\beta}_{0} + \widehat{\beta}_{1} \cdot \text{Age}
$$

- The $Y$ variable here is [*categorical*]{style="color:darkorchid;"} ([two levels]{style="color:darkorange;"}—every account in this data set is either labeled `Good` or `Bad`), so regular linear regression won’t work here.
- But what if we just [do it]{style="color:darkorange;"} anyway?

## Binary Variable

- Let’s first create a dummy variable `Bad` to convert Status to a quantitative dummy variable:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true

library(tidyverse)
banco = banco %>% 
  mutate(Bad = ifelse(banco$Status == "Bad", 1, 0))
```

- We could do this with 1 representing either [Bad]{style="color:darkorange;"} or [Good]{style="color:darkorange;"} (it wouldn’t matter). Here it makes sense to use 1 for `Bad`, since that is the outcome the bank wants to predict.

## Regular Linear Regression {.smaller}

```{r, fig.align = 'center'}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true

ggplot(banco, aes(x=Age, y = Bad)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se = F)
```

- A line is not a great fit to this data—it’s not even close to linear. And what does it mean to predict that `Bad` = 0.7 (or 1.2)?

## Logistic Regression

- Instead of predicting whether an account is [*Bad*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, let’s predict the [*probability*]{style="color:darkorange;"} that it is [*Bad*]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- In [*logistic regression*]{style="color:darkorange;"}, one level of $Y$ is always called [“success”]{style="color:darkorchid;"} and the other called [“failure.”]{style="color:darkorchid;"} Since $Y = 1$ for Bad accounts, in our setup we have designated Bad status as [“success.”]{style="color:darkorchid;"} (You could also set $Y = 1$ for Good accounts and call Good status “success.”)

- Let’s [fit a curve]{style="color:darkorange;"} that is always between 0 and 1.

## Odds and Probabilty {.smaller}

- To fit the Logistic regression model we need to know the difference between [**odds**]{style="color:darkorchid;"} and [**probability**]{style="color:darkorchid;"} and how they relate.

- When something has [“even (1/1) odds,”]{style="color:darkorange;"} the probability of success is 1/2.

- When something has [“2/1 odds,”]{style="color:darkorange;"} the probability of success is 2/3.

- When something has [“3/2 odds,”]{style="color:darkorange;"} the probability of success is 3/5.

- In general, the [**odds**]{style="color:darkorchid;"} of something happening are $p/(1 − p)$.

- Where $p$ is the [**probability**]{style="color:darkorchid;"} defined bewteen zero and one.

- You can transform odds to probability: $$
  \text{Odds} = \frac{3}{2} = \frac{3/(3+2)}{2/(3+2)} = \frac{3/5}{2/5}  = \frac{p}{1-p}
  $$

- If the odds are between zero and one they are not in your favor, $(1-p)>p$

- Let's the explore this relation!

## Probability vs odds vs log odds {.smaller}

| Probability $p$ | Odds $p/(1 − p)$ | Log odds $\log(p/(1 − p))$ |
|:---------------:|:----------------:|:--------------------------:|
|        0        |        0         |         $-\infty$          |
|      0.25       |       0.33       |           −1.10            |
|       0.5       |        1         |             0              |
|      0.75       |        3         |            1.10            |
|       0.8       |        4         |            1.39            |
|       0.9       |        9         |            2.20            |
|      0.95       |        19        |            2.94            |
|        1        |     $\infty$     |          $\infty$          |

- Probability is between [zero and one]{style="color:darkorange;"}.
- Odds are [strictly positive]{style="color:darkorange;"} (greater than zero).
- Log odds ranges the [whole real line]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

## The logistic regression model

- [Logistic regression]{style="color:darkorange;"} models the [**log odds**]{style="color:darkorchid;"} of success $p$ as a linear function of $X$: $$
  \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X + e
  $$

- This fits an "S-shaped" curve to the data

- We’ll see what it looks like later

- By making this choice, we have a series of benefits.

- Let’s try it!

## The logistic regression model {.smaller}

- We need a different function - `glm()` (generalized linear models)

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
model <- glm(Bad ~ Age, data = banco, family = binomial)
summary(model)
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
b = coef(model)   # b[1] = intercept, b[2] = Age
```

- How ca we interpret this model?

## The logistic regression model {.smaller}

- The logistic regression output tells us that our [prediction]{style="color:darkorange;"} is $$
  \log(\text{odds}) = \log\left(\frac{\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}}{1-\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}}\right) = `r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age}
  $$

- To get the probability we have to solve in terms $\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}$

- The [probability]{style="color:darkorange;"} of having a `Bad` status given `Age`: $$
  \widehat{p(\text{Bad})} = \frac{\exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age})}{1+ \exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age})}
  $$ where $\exp()$ is the exponential function $e^x$.

## Let's show this {.smaller}

Let $\widehat{p} = \widehat{p(\text{Bad})}$, and $\exp(X\widehat{\beta}) = \exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age})$:

$$
\begin{eqnarray}
\log\left(\frac{\widehat{p}}{1-\widehat{p}}\right) &=& X\widehat{\beta} \\
\exp\left(\log\left(\frac{\widehat{p}}{1-\widehat{p}}\right)\right) &=& \exp(X\widehat{\beta}) \\
\frac{\widehat{p}}{1-\widehat{p}} &=& \exp(X\widehat{\beta})\\ 
\widehat{p} &=& \exp(X\widehat{\beta})\cdot (1-\widehat{p})\\
\widehat{p} &=&\exp(X\widehat{\beta}) - \exp(X\widehat{\beta}) \cdot \widehat{p} \\
\widehat{p} &=& \frac{\exp(X\widehat{\beta})}{1 + \exp(X\widehat{\beta})}
\end{eqnarray}
$$

## Visualizing the model {.smaller}

```{r, fig.align = 'center'}
    ggplot(banco, aes(x=Age, y=Bad)) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_line(aes(x = Age, y = predict(model,type = "response")), color = "blue")
```

- How to interpret this curve?
- The blue line is $\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}$, given the `Age`.

## Interpreting the coefficients {.smaller}

Our [prediction equation]{style="color:darkorange;"} is:

$$
\log(\text{odds}) = \log\left(\frac{\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}}{1-\widehat{p(\text{Bad})}}\right) = `r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age}
$$

Let’s start with some basic, but [not particularly useful]{style="color:darkorange;"}, interpretations:

- When `Age` = 0, we predict that the log odds will be `r round(b[1], 2)`, so the probability of a bad status is predicted to be `r round(100 * plogis(b[1]), 1)`% (a customer with zero age is not meaningful).

- When `Age` increases by 1 year, we predict that the log odds of having a bad status will `r dir(b[2])` by `r abs(round(b[2], 2))`.

- Instead of [log odds]{style="color:darkorange;"} is better to have the interpretation in [odds]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

## Interpreting the coefficients {.smaller}

- Let’s rewrite the prediction equation as:

- [Predicted odds]{style="color:darkorange;"} of a bad status, $\exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot \text{Age})$.

- [Increasing age by 1]{style="color:darkorange;"} year will multiply the odds by $\exp(`r round(b[2], 2)`) = `r round(exp(b[2]), 2)`$; i.e., `r dir(b[2])` the odds by `r abs(pct(b[2]))`%.

- In summary, $$(\exp(\widehat{\beta}) - 1)\times 100 = \text{percentage change in odds}.$$

- [Increasing age by 2]{style="color:darkorange;"} years will multiply the odds by $\exp(2\cdot`r round(b[2], 2)`) = `r round(exp(2 * b[2]), 2)`$; i.e., `r dir(b[2])` the odds by `r abs(pct(2 * b[2]))`%.

- Odds equal to 1 indicate an one-to-one chance.

## Making predictions {.smaller}

- What is the [probability]{style="color:darkorange;"} of having a bad status given the customer has an age of 35.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
predict(model, list(Age=35), type="response")
```

- Using the probability equation in **R**:

$$
\widehat{p(\text{Bad})} = \frac{\exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot 35)}{1+ \exp(`r round(b[1], 2)` `r sgn(b[2])` \cdot 35)} = `r round(plogis(b[1] + b[2] * 35), 2)`
$$

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
exp(coef(model)[1] + coef(model)[2]*35)/(1+exp(coef(model)[1] + coef(model)[2]*35))
```

## Adding more predictors

- Adding another predictor: [can we do better?]{style="color:darkorange;"}

- Just like with a linear regression model, we can [add additional predictors]{style="color:darkorange;"} to the model (for example, `Other_Credit`).

- Our interpretation of the coefficients in multiple logistic regression is [similar to multiple linear regression]{style="color:darkorange;"}, in the sense that each coefficient represents the predicted effect of one $X$ on $Y$, [holding the other]{style="color:darkorange;"} $X$ variables constant.

## How good is our model?

- Unfortunately, the typical root mean squared error, [RSE metric isn’t available for logistic regression]{style="color:darkorchid;"}.
- However, there are [many metrics]{style="color:darkorchid;"} that indicate model fit.
- But: most of these metrics are difficult to interpret, so we’ll focus on [something simpler]{style="color:darkorange;"} to interpret and communicate.

## Accuracy of the model {.smaller}

- We could use our model to [make a prediction]{style="color:darkorange;"} of [Status]{style="color:darkorange;"} based on the probability.

- Suppose we say that our prediction is: $$
  \text{Prediction} = \begin{cases}
  \text{Bad}, & \text{if $\widehat{P(\text{Bad})} \geq 0.5$}, \\
  \text{Good}, & \text{if $\widehat{P(\text{Bad})} < 0.5$}. \\
  \end{cases}
  $$

- Given a threshold of 0.5, now we can compute the [fraction of accounts]{style="color:darkorange;"} whose status we [correctly predicted]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

- For Bad and Good accounts.

- This is known as the [**accuracy**]{style="color:darkorange;"} of the model.

## Accuracy of the model {.smaller}

- We can use the `xtabs` function to get the [**accuracy**]{style="color:darkorange;"}:

- We [add]{style="color:darkorange;"} we the number of [correctly predicted groups]{style="color:darkorange;"} for both Bad and Good, and divide by the total of observations.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
banco = banco %>% 
  mutate(predict.Status = factor(ifelse(predict(model, type="response") >= 0.5,"Bad","Good"),
                                 levels = c("Bad", "Good")))
xtabs(~ predict.Status + Status, banco) %>%
  addmargins()
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
cm = table(predict.Status = banco$predict.Status,
           Status = factor(banco$Status, levels = c("Bad", "Good")))
TP = cm["Bad", "Bad"];  TN = cm["Good", "Good"]
FP = cm["Bad", "Good"]; FN = cm["Good", "Bad"]
n = sum(cm); n_bad = sum(cm[, "Bad"]); n_good = sum(cm[, "Good"])
```

- Correctly predicted that is Good - `r TN`
- Correctly predicted that is Bad - `r TP`
- Total number of accounts in the sample - `r n`
- The [**accuracy**]{style="color:darkorange;"} is (`r TN` + `r TP`)/`r n` = `r round((TN + TP) / n, 3)`, or `r round(100 * (TN + TP) / n)`%

## Confusion Matrix {.smaller}

- The table from `xtabs` is also called a [Confusion matrix]{style="color:darkorange;"}

|                        | Actual failure | Actual success |
|:----------------------:|:--------------:|:--------------:|
| Model predicts failure | True negative  | False negative |
| Model predicts success | False positive | True positive  |

- [True positives]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting Bad for an account that is Bad
- [True negatives]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting Good for an account that is Good
- [False positives]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting Bad for an account that is Good
- [False negatives]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting Good for an account that is Bad
- If we had designated Good as 1 and Bad as 0, these would have switched
- So **Accuracy** = (True negative + True positive)/(Total cases)

## Accuracy of the model {.smaller}

Suppose that the Amazon is trying to build a model to [predict which customers buy a certain product]{style="color:darkorchid;"}:

- Suppose that 0.01% of people are customers of this product (the product is really expensive / high revenue)

- A “null” or “no-brainer” model that predicts that [no one]{style="color:darkorange;"} is a customer will be 99.99% accurate.

- The revenue coming from our model would be zero.

- But the model could make two different kinds of prediction errors:

- [*False positive*]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting someone is a customer when they really are not

- [*False negative*]{style="color:darkorange;"}: predicting someone is not a customer when they really are

- These two measures give us a better idea of the predictive power of our model.

## False positive rate {.smaller}

The false positive rate is the proportion of actual failures where the model predicted success.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
xtabs(~ predict.Status + Status, banco) %>%
  addmargins()
```

- [False Positives]{style="color:darkorange;"} - predicting an account is Bad when it really is Good
- [Actual failure]{style="color:darkorange;"} - number of cases that are Good
- [**False positive rate**]{style="color:darkorange;"} = False positives/ Actual failure
- In our model, the false positive rate is `r FP`/`r n_good` = `r round(FP / n_good, 2)`

## False negative rate {.smaller}

The false negative rate is the proportion of actual successes where the model predicted failure.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
xtabs(~ predict.Status + Status, banco) %>%
  addmargins()
```

- [False Negatives]{style="color:darkorange;"} - predicting an account is Good when it really is Bad
- [Actual success]{style="color:darkorange;"} - number of cases that are Bad
- [**False negative rate**]{style="color:darkorange;"} = False negatives/ Actual success
- In our model, the [false negative rate]{style="color:darkorange;"} is `r FN`/`r n_bad` = `r round(FN / n_bad, 2)`

## Changing rates {.smaller}

How do we reduce false [positive/negative]{style="color:darkorange;"} rates?

- Instead of using [50%]{style="color:darkorange;"} as a cutoff probability to decide when to predict success, use a higher (or lower) probability.
- For example, we could have the model predict that an account is Bad only if $\widehat{p(\text{Bad})} \geq 0.8$, instead of 0.5:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| output: true
banco = banco %>% 
  mutate(predict.Status = factor(ifelse(predict(model, type="response") >= 0.8,"Bad","Good"),
                                 levels = c("Bad", "Good")))
xtabs(~ predict.Status + Status,banco) %>%
  addmargins()
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
cm8 = table(predict.Status = banco$predict.Status,
            Status = factor(banco$Status, levels = c("Bad", "Good")))
TP8 = cm8["Bad", "Bad"];  TN8 = cm8["Good", "Good"]
FP8 = cm8["Bad", "Good"]; FN8 = cm8["Good", "Bad"]
```

- [Accuracy]{style="color:darkorange;"} = (`r TN8`+`r TP8`)/`r n` = `r round((TN8 + TP8) / n, 2)`
- [False positive rate]{style="color:darkorange;"} = `r FP8`/`r n_good` = `r round(FP8 / n_good, 2)`
- [False negative rate]{style="color:darkorange;"} = `r FN8`/`r n_bad` = `r round(FN8 / n_bad, 2)`

## Prediction Trade off

- We can [decrease]{style="color:darkorange;"} the [false positive rate]{style="color:darkorange;"}, but at the expense of [increasing]{style="color:darkorange;"} the [false negative rate]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

- Or we can [decrease the false negative rate]{style="color:darkorange;"}, but at the expense of increasing the false positive rate.

- We might choose a [cutoff probability other than 50%]{style="color:darkorange;"} based on our assessment of the relative costs of the two different kinds of errors.

- For the bank, approving a customer who later has a `Bad` account (a false negative) may be more costly than turning away a customer who would have been `Good` (a false positive).

## Summary

In a [logistic regression model]{style="color:darkorange;"}, the response variable is binary, taking values of either zero or one.

- The model estimates the [log odds]{style="color:darkorange;"} of the event associated with a response of one.

- The model's effects are interpreted in terms of [odds]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

- Predictions are expressed as [probabilities]{style="color:darkorange;"}.

- The performance of the model is evaluated based on its prediction [accuracy]{style="color:darkorange;"}.
